title: The minor rules
hook: the Buddha allowed minor rules to be dropped, but no one asked which; the elders kept them all

segments.voice: Yesterday: thus have I heard, a teaching held in people before it was written. Your line: the binding of an unwritten book. Today, one thing nobody remembered to ask.

Which rules are minor? It sounds like a small question. In the account of the Buddha's last days, he tells Ananda that after he is gone, the community may, if it wishes, set aside the lesser and minor rules. It's a generous permission, a teacher loosening his grip and trusting his students. But it comes with a gap in it, and at the first council, the gap opens.
screen: `WHICH RULES ARE MINOR?` → `YOU MAY SET THEM ASIDE.` → `A GAP IN THE PERMISSION.`

segments.voice: At the council, Ananda tells the elders what the Buddha said: the minor rules may be dropped. The elders ask the obvious thing. Which ones? Did you ask him? Ananda says no. He didn't ask. The Vinaya lets us hear the elders trying. Some say every rule except the gravest ones is minor. Others draw the line a little higher, then higher again. Each answer is reasonable. None of them settles it, because the one person who could settle it is gone. Then Mahakassapa turns the question around. Lay people know which things are proper for monks, he says. If we start dropping rules now, they'll say the teacher's rules lasted only as long as the teacher, like smoke. So let us not add rules the Buddha didn't make, and not take away rules he did make. The elders agree. They kept them all. It cost Ananda something. After the council, the elders name several things he did wrong, and failing to ask which rules were minor is one of them. Ananda says he didn't see it as a fault, but out of trust in the elders he acknowledges it. Some readers hear the elders being hard on him. Others hear the community choosing steadiness over its own best guess. Either way, the council kept the whole set of rules, and in the Theravada telling, that is why the small rules are still kept alongside the great ones.
screen: `DID YOU ASK HIM WHICH?` · `SOME DRAW THE LINE HERE, SOME THERE.` · `NOT ADD, NOT TAKE AWAY.` · `ANANDA ACKNOWLEDGES IT.` · then, large: `THEY KEPT THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: Choose one small rule you already live by, or used to: closing the cupboard, answering a message the same day. Decide to keep it fully today, not because it's important but because you said you would, and picture the moment it will come up.
Mahakassapa. He argued that no rule should be added or dropped, since the one person who could say which were minor was gone. Today's word.
Your line: they kept them all. Not add, not take away. Day eight hundred fifty-three, done.

howItsDone: Theravada monks keep the full code of monastic rules, minor ones included, and recite it together at regular gatherings of the community.

original.note: Pali: the lesser and minor, the words used for the rules the Buddha said could be set aside.

trapdoor: what you thought: some rules don't really matter.
what it means: the Buddha allowed small rules to be dropped, but no one knew which, so the elders kept every one.
what a scholar hears: Digha Nikaya 16 gives the permission and Cullavagga 11 the council's refusal to use it; the elders' different guesses show the question was open from the start.

chat.says: If the Buddha let them drop minor rules, why did the monks keep them all?
options: No one knew which rules he meant, so they chose to add none and drop none.
The Buddha took the permission back before he died, so none could go.
The elders decided every rule was major, so the permission didn't apply.
chat.meaning: Ananda never asked which rules were minor. Mahakassapa proposed adding none and dropping none, and the elders agreed.

Mahakassapa.meaning: the elder who proposed keeping every rule

Ananda.meaning: the Buddha's attendant, who never asked which rules

Theravada.meaning: the school of the elders, with its canon in Pali

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta), the lesser and minor rules
Vinaya, Cullavagga 11.1.9–10 (the minor rules and Ananda's faults)

notes: Elders' guesses summarized without naming categories (parajika, sanghadisesa, etc.) or counts; confirm the summary 'every rule except the gravest ones ... a little higher, then higher again' is fair.
Mahakassapa's 'like smoke' simile: paraphrased from Cullavagga 11.1.9; confirm.
Ananda's faults: confirm he acknowledged them out of faith in the elders while not seeing them as faults himself.
'That choice still shapes how Theravada monks live' is a general description of Theravada practice; confirm. Other schools' Vinayas tell the episode similarly, not addressed here.
